text.tspan: CHOOSING THE RIGHT SURFACE · APPLE WATCH
A case study in solving for the right surface. Tracking lifts is a phone job
until you're at the rack, where the phone is the one thing you can't reach.
So the real design work wasn't another app screen; it was moving the
but no until to the rack.
I tracked lifts on my phone for months. It held the data fine but the phone is the one thing I
never have in hand mid-set. It's on the bench, in a bag, across the room. So the moment I
actually needed last week's numbers, they were exactly where I couldn't reach.
the phone is the last thing you
want to dig out, unlock, and
The number I needed, what I
lifted last time was buried in
history, two taps away, at the
Without last time in front of
me, I'd lift roughly the same
“The watch is already on my wrist for the whole workout. That's where the number needs to live.”
This isn't the whole app shrunk onto a wrist. The phone and the watch each do the
single thing they're actually good at and the hand-off between them is the design.
The phone stays the source of truth; the watch owns the workout itself.

Three rules the wrist had to respect.
A watch screen is tiny, read while breathing hard, operated with one chalky
thumb. I wrote these three down before drawing anything, in priority order, to
Memory at the moment of use
Last session's numbers appear on the logging screen
itself, not buried in history. This is the founding promise;
any decision that hides it is wrong by definition.
You can't type at the rack. The Digital Crown does the
work, dial a number that's already close, glance,
confirm. Every interaction survives fatigue and chalk.
The watch remembers so you don't have to. But it still
makes you choose the number. Recall without a rubber-
stamp; you stay the one deciding to push.
Dial up from what you did,
When a set's logging cell becomes active, the
Digital Crown is pre-loaded to last session's
number 75 kg, not blank. A small line above
reads "Last · 75 kg × 8". So the decision isn't
"what did I do?" that's answered it's only "do I
match it or beat it?" One turn of the Crown and
you're at 77.5. Recall and input collapse into a
single motion, and the founding promise lives
A whole session on the wrist, in four phases: the workout arrives, you log
each set with two quick dials, move freely between exercises, and finish. The
seven screens group into the rhythm you actually feel at the gym.
Start the workout arrives from your phone
You tap Start on the phone and the planned session lands on the wrist — exercises,
set counts, and last session’s numbers, all queued. Nothing to set up; the watch
already knows the plan. This is the last time the phone is involved.
Log a set, two dials and a rest, no keyboard
The core loop, repeated for every set. Weight and reps each get their own single-value
screen so the Crown is never ambiguous it pre-loads on last session’s number, you dial and
confirm. Logging then starts the rest timer on its own. Splitting the two values is the fix for
an earlier design where one Crown couldn’t serve both cells at once.
Move through the workout in any order
Real sessions aren’t a straight line: equipment’s taken, you superset, you change your mind.
The exercise name opens the full list, where each lift shows its progress green done,
orange half-finished, hollow untouched. Jump anywhere; each exercise remembers where
you left off and reopens on its next unlogged set. Moving is free; editing the plan stays on
A clean completion state with any new PRs called out, then the whole session writes back
to the phone, where History and Analytics update from real logged data. The phone is the
record; the watch did the work you never reached for it once.
Letting you move through the workout in any order is essential at the rack.
Letting you rewrite it, add, remove, reorder exercises is not. I prototyped it,
and it dragged phone-sized complexity onto a glanceable screen. So the line
is deliberate, free navigation on the watch, plan editing stays on the phone.
The watch is a runner, not an editor.
